## Legal research memo

**Conclusion.** Assuming New York law governs and the client acted as a finder, the oral 3% promise is likely unenforceable.

New York General Obligations Law § 5-701(a)(10) requires a writing subscribed by the seller or its agent for a promise to pay for services in the sale of a business. The statute expressly includes *introducing* a party to the transaction. The client’s introduction therefore falls within the rule. [N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-701(a)(10)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/5-701); [*Intercontinental Planning, Ltd. v. Daystrom, Inc.*, 24 N.Y.2d 372, 378–80 (1969)](https://openjurist.org/24/ny2d/372/intercontinental-planning-ltd-v-daystrom-inc).

Closing the sale does not cure the missing writing: part performance does not remove this type of agreement from § 5-701. Nor can the client recover the fee by calling it quantum meruit or unjust enrichment. [*Best Global Alternative, Ltd. v. FCIC Construction Services, Inc.*, 170 A.D.3d 1101, 1102–03 (2d Dep’t 2019)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2019/2019_02308.htm); [*Snyder v. Bronfman*, 13 N.Y.3d 504, 508–09 (2009)](https://www.nycourts.gov/REPORTER/3dseries/2009/2009_08667.htm).

Review the seller’s signed communications and sale documents for a memorandum covering this transaction and the agreed 3% rate. An admission by the seller of the agreement’s essential terms could also change the result; a refusal to pay, by itself, establishes no such admission. [*Stone Capital Advisors, LLC v. Fortrend International, LLC*, 15 A.D.3d 300, 301 (1st Dep’t 2005)](https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/appellate-division-first-department/2005/2005-01289.html); [*Camhi v. Tedesco Realty, LLC*, 105 A.D.3d 795, 797 (2d Dep’t 2013)](https://www.nycourts.gov/REPORTER/3dseries/2013/2013_02368.htm).

## Legal research memo

**Conclusion.** Assuming New York law applies and the client is an ordinary finder, the oral 3% promise is unenforceable. New York General Obligations Law § 5-701(a)(10) requires a writing signed by the seller for a promise to pay for services in the sale of a business. The statute expressly includes *introducing* a party to the transaction. [N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-701(a)(10)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/5-701).

The completed sale does not cure the missing writing. The Court of Appeals applies the statute to compensation for finding a business acquisition and bars attempts to recover the same fee through quantum meruit or unjust enrichment. [*Snyder v. Bronfman*, 13 N.Y.3d 504, 508–10 (2009)](https://www.nycourts.gov/REPORTER/3dseries/2009/2009_08667.htm). Part performance likewise does not remove a claim from § 5-701’s writing requirement. [*Kelly v. P & G Ventures 1, LLC*, 148 A.D.3d 1002, 1004 (2d Dep’t 2017)](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2017/2017_02026.htm).

**Next inquiry.** Review the seller’s emails and signed closing documents. A signed memorandum acknowledging the finder’s role may satisfy the statute even if it omits the fee rate; in that event, recovery may be for reasonable value rather than necessarily 3%. [*Morris Cohon & Co. v. Russell*, 23 N.Y.2d 569, 574–76 (1969)](https://openjurist.org/23/ny2d/569/morris-cohon-co-v-russell). The statute also exempts compensation contracts with a duly licensed real estate broker or salesperson, an attorney, or an auctioneer. On the stated handshake facts, with no qualifying writing or exemption, the seller need not pay the promised fee.

**Authorities cited**

[N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-701(a)(10)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/5-701)

**Legal research memo**

**Question.** Does filing proof of “nail and mail” service 45 days after affixing and mailing invalidate service, and when is the answer due?

**Analysis.** The filing missed the 20-day deadline in [CPLR 308(4)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/308). But in the Second Department, which includes Queens, late proof does **not by itself invalidate otherwise proper service**. It is a procedural defect the court may cure without prejudicing the defendant. [*Penachio v Penachio*](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2006/2006_01782.htm); [*Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Welz*](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2022/2022_07477.htm). The facts given do not establish that service was otherwise proper: the server must first have exercised due diligence to attempt personal or substituted delivery, affixed the summons at a qualifying address, and mailed it as the statute requires. [*Ramirez v Escobar*](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2024/2024_03193.htm); CPLR 308(4).

**Deadline, assuming the summons and complaint were served together:** In Supreme Court, service becomes complete 10 days after proof is filed; the answer is due 30 days later—**40 days after filing, or day 85 after affixing and mailing**. CPLR 308(4); [CPLR 3012(c)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/3012). A court order curing the late filing may set a protective deadline. *Welz*.

If this is a **New York City Civil Court** action, the different rule is **30 days after proof is filed—day 75**. [CCA 402(b)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CCA/402); [CCA 409](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CCA/409); [*Rodriguez v Rodriguez*](https://www.nycourts.gov/REPORTER/3dseries/2012/2012_08713.htm). If only a summons was served, these are appearance or demand-for-complaint deadlines; the answer deadline depends on service of the complaint. CPLR 3012(b).

**Legal research memo (New York).** Assuming the summons and complaint were served, the answer depends on which Queens court hears the case.

**Queens Supreme Court.** CPLR 308(4) permits affixing and mailing only after due diligence to use the methods in subdivisions (1) and (2), and requires proof of service within 20 days of the later step. Filing on day 45 is late. That delay does not itself defeat personal jurisdiction if the affixing and mailing otherwise complied with the statute, but the late filing alone does not complete service or start the answer period. The defendant therefore has **no answer deadline yet and is not in default**. The court may cure the filing defect under CPLR 2004; it must then give the defendant a fair opportunity to answer, ordinarily 30 days after service of the curing order. [CPLR 308(4)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/308); [CPLR 320(a)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/320); [*First Fed. Sav. & Loan Assn. of Charleston v Tezzi*, 164 A.D.3d 758 (2d Dep’t 2018)](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2018/2018_05826.htm).

**Queens Civil Court.** Its separate statute sets **no 20-day deadline** for filing proof. If the affixing and mailing were otherwise proper, service became complete when proof was filed on day 45, and the answer is due **30 days after that filing—day 75**. [NYC Civil Court Act §§ 402(b), 409, 410(b)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CCA/402); [*Rodriguez v Rodriguez*, 103 A.D.3d 117 (2d Dep’t 2012)](https://www.nycourts.gov/REPORTER/3dseries/2012/2012_08713.htm).

**Legal research memo — New York security deposit**

**Conclusion.** Under current law, a new market-rate or rent-stabilized residential lease generally cannot require a security deposit exceeding one month’s rent. The tenant can seek return of the unlawful second month. N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law §§ [7-108(1-a)(a)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/7-108), [7-107(2)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/7-107).

The landlord has **14 days after the tenant vacates** to provide an itemized statement explaining any amount retained and to return the balance. No statement is required *at move-out itself*. If the 14 days have passed without a statement, the landlord forfeits the right to retain **any** of the deposit; the tenant can seek return of both months, even if the landlord later alleges damage. N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law §§ 7-108(1-a)(e), 7-107(6); [*Cohen v. Abruzzo*, 225 A.D.3d 723 (2d Dep’t 2024)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2024/2024_03163.htm).

The tenant may sue for the withheld deposit as actual damages. A court may award **additional punitive damages of up to twice the deposit** if the violation was willful; failure to itemize alone does not establish willfulness. N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law §§ 7-108(1-a)(g), 7-107(8); [*Case v. 575 Classon Ave., LLC*, 81 Misc. 3d 144(A) (App. Term, 2d Dep’t 2024)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2024/2024_50199.htm). The apartment’s regulatory status and the move-out date should be confirmed.

**Authorities cited**

[N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-107](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/7-107)  
[N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 7-108](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/7-108)

**Legal research memo**

Assuming an ordinary residential rental rather than a rent controlled unit or another statutory exception, the landlord could demand **no more than one month’s rent** as a security deposit. The second month was unlawfully collected. The same cap applies to rent stabilized apartments. [N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law §§ 7-108(1-a)(a), 7-107(2)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/7-108).

After the tenant vacates, the landlord has **14 days** to provide an itemized statement of any deductions and return the balance. Permitted deductions are limited to specified costs such as unpaid rent and tenant caused damage beyond ordinary wear. If the landlord provides no timely statement, it forfeits the right to retain **any** of the deposit, including the otherwise permissible first month. [N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law §§ 7-108(1-a)(b), (e), 7-107(3), (6)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/7-108); [*Cohen v. Abruzzo*, 228 A.D.3d 724 (2d Dep’t 2024)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2024/2024_03163.htm).

The tenant can demand the full two month deposit and sue for its return if the 14 days have passed. A **willful** violation may also support punitive damages of up to twice the deposit, but those damages are not automatic; an innocent violation did not warrant them in *Prando*. [N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law §§ 7-108(1-a)(g), 7-107(8)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/7-108); [*Prando v. Kelly*, 73 Misc. 3d 144(A) (App. Term, 2d Dep’t 2021)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2021/2021_51241.htm).

**Legal research memo (New York).** One witness being present when the decedent signed does **not**, by itself, invalidate the will. New York permits the testator to sign before each witness, or acknowledge her signature to each witness, separately. But an ordinary will requires **two attesting witnesses**: she must declare to each that the document is her will, and both must sign at her request within one 30-day period. [EPTL § 3-2.1(a)(2)–(4)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/EPT/3-2.1). The will’s proponent bears the burden of proving due execution. [*Matter of Robbins*, 206 A.D.3d 739, 740 (2d Dep’t 2022)](https://www.nycourts.gov/REPORTER/3dseries/2022/2022_03729.htm); [*Matter of Mele*, 113 A.D.3d 858, 859 (2d Dep’t 2014)](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2014/2014_00512.htm).

Thus, **if only one person ever attested**, the will cannot be admitted as an ordinary will. If a second witness later received the required acknowledgment and declaration and signed within the statutory period, the fact that only one witnessed the original signing is no defect. The limited holographic-will exception requires facts not supplied here. [EPTL § 3-2.2](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/EPT/3-2.2).

Assuming the will is invalid and no earlier valid will controls, the **net probate estate** passes by intestacy. The husband receives the first **$50,000 plus half the remainder**; the two surviving children divide the other half equally, so each receives **one-quarter of the remainder**. If the net estate is $50,000 or less, the husband takes it all. [EPTL § 4-1.1(a)(1)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/EPT/4-1.1).

[*Matter of Mele*, 113 A.D.3d 858 (2d Dep’t 2014)](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2014/2014_00512.htm)

**Legal research memo (New York).** One witness **present when the decedent signed** does not, by itself, make the will invalid. The testator may sign or acknowledge her signature to each witness separately. For an ordinary will, she must also declare the document to be her will to each witness, and at least two witnesses must attest and sign at her request within one 30-day period. *EPTL* § 3-2.1(a)(2)–(4). The proponent bears the burden of proving due execution. *Matter of Nires*, 241 A.D.3d 555 (2d Dep’t 2025).

If **only one witness ever attested**, the will fails that requirement and cannot be probated. *Matter of Karschmidt*, 26 Misc. 3d 905, 907–08 (Sur. Ct. Westchester Cnty. 2009). This assumes the limited exception for certain military personnel and mariners does not apply. *EPTL* § 3-2.2.

If there is no earlier valid will, the **probate estate**, after debts and administration and reasonable funeral expenses, passes by intestacy. The husband receives the first **$50,000 plus half of the remainder**; the two surviving children receive **one quarter of the remainder each**. If the distributable estate is $50,000 or less, the husband receives it all. *EPTL* § 4-1.1(a)(1).

## Legal research memo

**Question.** Is a New York malpractice claim timely when a surgeon left a sponge in a patient in 2021 and the patient discovered it in March 2026?

**Conclusion.** **Likely yes, if filed by the corresponding date in March 2027**, provided the patient did not earlier discover facts that would reasonably have led to the sponge’s discovery. New York ordinarily requires a medical malpractice action within two years and six months of the alleged error. Its foreign-object exception instead permits suit within one year of actual discovery or discovery of facts reasonably leading to it, whichever is earlier. [CPLR 214-a(a)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/214-A).

A sponge inadvertently left after surgery is a foreign object under the Court of Appeals’ rule. [*Flanagan v. Mount Eden General Hospital*, 24 N.Y.2d 427, 431 (1969)](https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/court-of-appeals/1969/24-n-y-2d-427-0.html); [*Walton v. Strong Memorial Hospital*, 25 N.Y.3d 554, 571–73 (2015)](https://www.nycourts.gov/REPORTER/3dseries/2015/2015_04786.htm). The 2021 surgery therefore does not itself make this claim late. Whether earlier symptoms or records started the one-year clock depends on what the patient knew; symptoms alone did not establish earlier discoverability in a retained-sponge case. [*Baker v. Eastern Niagara Hospital, Inc.*, 217 A.D.3d 1331, 1333–34 (4th Dep’t 2023)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2023/2023_03090.htm).

**Hospital-status qualification.** If the defendant is a municipal hospital, a separate notice of claim generally must be served within 90 days after the claim arises. That period may have passed for a March 2026 discovery, though a court may allow late notice. The hospital’s ownership and any notice already served must be checked before calling the claim timely against that defendant. [General Municipal Law § 50-e(1)(a), (5)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GMU/50-E); [*Melendez v. City of New York*, 249 A.D.2d 197, 198 (1st Dep’t 1998)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/files/bv/249AD2d.pdf).

**Legal research memo — September 28, 2026**

**A malpractice suit filed now is likely timely.** New York ordinarily requires filing within two years and six months of the alleged malpractice. But a claim based on a foreign object left in a patient may be filed within one year after the patient discovers it *or* discovers facts that would reasonably lead to its discovery, whichever occurs first. [CPLR 214-a(a)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/214-A).

A sponge accidentally left after surgery qualifies for that exception. The Court of Appeals recognized the rule for retained surgical instruments in [*Flanagan v. Mount Eden General Hospital*, 24 N.Y.2d 427 (1969)](https://openjurist.org/24/ny2d/427/flanagan-v-mount-eden-general-hospital), and the Appellate Division applied it to retained surgical sponges in [*Baker v. Eastern Niagara Hospital*, 217 A.D.3d 1331 (4th Dep’t 2023)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2023/2023_03090.htm). If March 2026 was the first discovery date under the statute, the filing deadline is the corresponding date in **March 2027**. Earlier medical findings that reasonably pointed to the sponge could move that deadline earlier.

**Hospital status matters.** A claim against a municipal hospital may also require a notice of claim within 90 days of accrual; the ordinary notice period following March discovery has passed, though a court may permit late notice. [General Municipal Law § 50-e(1), (5)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GMU/50-E); [*Melendez v. City of New York*, 249 A.D.2d 197 (1st Dep’t 1998)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/files/bv/249AD2d.pdf).

**Legal research memo (New York law)**

**Question.** May a New York LLC formed in 2023 sue a customer in Supreme Court for an unpaid invoice if it never completed publication?

**Conclusion.** It should complete publication and file proof with the Department of State **before suing**. Limited Liability Company Law § 206(a) requires publication in two designated newspapers for six successive weeks and filing a certificate of publication with the newspapers’ affidavits. Failure to file within 120 days suspends the LLC’s authority to conduct business in New York. The Appellate Division has held that a noncompliant LLC cannot maintain an action in New York; a complaint is subject to dismissal for lack of capacity under CPLR 3211(a)(3). *Small Step Day Care, LLC v. Broadway Bushwick Bldrs., L.P.*, 137 A.D.3d 1102, 1103 (2d Dep’t 2016); see *Barklee Realty Co. v. Pataki*, 309 A.D.2d 310, 311 (1st Dep’t 2003).

The missed 2023 deadline does **not** invalidate the customer’s contract or erase the invoice. Section 206(a) permits late compliance: once the LLC files substantially compliant proof of publication, its suspension is annulled. Thus, it can pursue the debt after completing and filing the publication materials.

**Authorities cited**

[N.Y. Limited Liability Company Law § 206(a)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/LLC/206)  
[N.Y. CPLR 3211(a)(3)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/3211)  
[*Small Step Day Care, LLC v. Broadway Bushwick Bldrs., L.P.*, 137 A.D.3d 1102 (2d Dep’t 2016)](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2016/2016_02071.htm)  
[*Barklee Realty Co. v. Pataki*, 309 A.D.2d 310 (1st Dep’t 2003)](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ny-supreme-court-appellate-division/1046994.html)

**Legal research memo**

**Question.** May a New York LLC formed in 2023 sue a customer in New York Supreme Court for an unpaid invoice if it never completed publication?

**Answer.** It may file a complaint, but a timely capacity objection puts the suit at substantial risk of dismissal. [Limited Liability Company Law § 206(a)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/LLC/206) requires six weeks of publication in two designated newspapers and filing a certificate of publication with the Department of State. Failure to file within 120 days suspends the LLC’s authority to conduct business in New York. The statute expressly preserves its contracts, so the unpaid invoice remains enforceable; late filing annuls the suspension.

The Appellate Division held that an LLC’s failure to comply with § 206 precluded it from bringing a contract action and affirmed dismissal for lack of capacity. [*Small Step Day Care, LLC v Broadway Bushwick Bldrs., L.P.*, 137 AD3d 1102, 1103 (2d Dept 2016)](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2016/2016_02071.htm). A recent Supreme Court decision likewise dismissed a contract suit **without prejudice** even though the LLC completed publication after suing. [*Credit League, LLC v Cella Bella’s Hospice Corp.*, 2026 NY Slip Op 31905(U) (Sup Ct, Kings County 2026)](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/pdfs/2026/2026_31905.pdf). Trial courts differ on whether completion during a pending case avoids dismissal, so the LLC should complete publication and file the certificate **before** suing.

This is a capacity defense, not an invalidation of the invoice. The customer generally waives it unless raised in a preanswer motion or answer. [CPLR 3211(a)(3), (e)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/3211).
